chunks.text: Inclusion of Neil J Gillespie for US Senate Website in the Library of Congress Web Archives On September 18, 2026 the United States Library of Congress informed me that my campaign website https://neilgillespie4senate.blogspot.com/ was selected for inclusion in the United States Election 2026 Web Archive.

chunks.title: Neil J. Gillespie for U.S. Senate
chunks.text: I believe my Notice to The Florida Bar: Anti-Weaponization Fund Federal Lawsuit , substantiates my Complaint of Election Fraud in the 2020 Election of Joe Biden and Kamala Harris (based on the Rule of Law , Separation of Powers Doctrine of Checks and Balances ) filed with the Federal Election Commission , and the Supreme Court of the United States ( PDF ), with Notice to President Trump ( PDF ), is of special interest to We The People , my campaign for United States Senate , and my campaign Neil2028 ( currently paused ).

chunks.title: Neil J. Gillespie for U.S. Senate
chunks.text: The United States Library of Congress has selected your website for inclusion in the United States Election 2026 Web Archive, which is part of a larger collection of historically and culturally significant websites that have been designated for preservation. The following URL has been selected: https://neilgillespie4senate.blogspot.com/.

chunks.title: Neil J. Gillespie for U.S. Senate
chunks.text: The Library of Congress or its agent will engage in the collection of content from your website at regular intervals over time. In order to properly archive the above URL, we may archive other portions of the website and public content that your page links to on third party sites such as social media platforms. In addition to the aforementioned collection, archived content from your website may be added to other relevant collections in the future. This content will be available to researchers at Library facilities and by special arrangement.

chunks.title: Neil J. Gillespie for U.S. Senate
chunks.text: It may also become more broadly available through hosting on the Library’s public website, which would be done no sooner than one year after it was collected. For more information on the web archiving process, please read our frequently asked questions.

chunks.title: Neil J. Gillespie for U.S. Senate
chunks.text: The Library hopes that you share its vision of preserving digital content and making it available to current and future generations of researchers. As the internet has become an increasingly important and influential part of our lives, we believe the historical record would be incomplete if websites like yours are not preserved and made a part of it. We encourage you to learn more about the Library’s Web Archiving Program and explore our collections to see examples of how we archive websites. If you have any questions, comments, or recommendations concerning the archiving of your website, please email the Library's Web Archiving Program at webcapture@loc.gov.

chunks.text: I am "No Party Neil", Neil J. Gillespie, a No Party Affiliation Candidate (NPA) for United States Senator for Florida in the general election set for November 3, 2026. I am motivated to run for office because of lawfare and lack of due process in our state and federal courts. Our first president, George Washington, warned us about political parties in his Farewell Address. That is why I am a "No Party Affiliation" (NPA) candidate. Washington emphasized three points: 1) The importance of unity as a Nation; 2) The danger of party loyalty over the interests of our Nation; 3) The danger of foreign entanglements.

chunks.title: Neil J. Gillespie for U.S. Senate
chunks.text: Regarding experience, I am founder and director of Justice Network, engaged in advocacy, education, news gathering and dissemination, and helping people fight injustice. I moved to Florida from Pennsylvania in 1993 where I was a licensed motor vehicle dealer. I am a capitalist. I am a graduate of the Wharton School, Evening Division, of the University of Pennsylvania (ABA), and of The Evergreen State College (BA). If elected, my top priorities are restore integrity in our government through the separation of powers doctrine. U.S. District Judge Pamela Chen says "The concept of separation of powers is what makes America great.

chunks.text: 1. Restore checks and balances in government, separation of powers. Lawyers admitted to practice are officers of the court, part of the judicial branch of government, and must not serve in elected office in the legislature or executive branch. Joe Biden and Kamala Harris, are lawyers admitted to practice, and who wrongly served as president and vice president, created the current immigration problem with open borders. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, a lawyer admitted to practice, is wrongly serving in the executive (as governor), and was able to wrongly take $10 million in taxpayer money, his "cherry on top", for his wife's charity.

chunks.title: Neil J. Gillespie for U.S. Senate
chunks.text: 2. Health care reform. I was born needing craniofacial surgery but my insurance denied coverage for surgery when I was age 18 under a preexisting condition clause. I propose national health coverage, with the ability to opt-out. Trial Lawyers add excessive costs, and force doctors to practice defensive medicine. See my Healthcare page https://www.nosue.org/healthcare/ Five other capitalist democracies -- the United Kingdom, Japan, Germany, Taiwan and Switzerland -- deliver health care to their people. We The People can learn from their successes and their failures.

chunks.title: Neil J. Gillespie for U.S. Senate
chunks.text: House and Senate members are allowed to purchase health insurance offered through the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, which covers more than 8 million federal workers.

chunks.text: 3. Guarantee the safety of Jews in the United States. America is the promised land that defeated fascism in Europe in 1945. Hold Bibi responsible for allowing October 7th to happen, and for the war on Iran. Iran is Bibi's war, and it is a disaster. Unfortunately, Israel cannot protect Jews. Its wars are creating antisemitism worldwide. Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin made peace with the Palestinians (Oslo Accords). chunks.text: Scott Pelley : Six firms in six weeks. Including Mark Elias's former firm. President Trump : This is an absolute honor to say what they've done is. chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Scott Pelley : The orders threaten to bar attorneys from where they work, courthouses and federal agencies. And cancel the contracts of law firm clients. For example, an aerospace company could lose its federal contracts if it stayed with the firm. A senior partner at one firm told us the president's orders were "diabolical", intended to bankrupt us. He said within hours his major clients were threatening to drop his firm. It took only a matter of days before America's wealthiest and most powerful law firms buckled. In a shock to the legal community, nine major firms went to the White House to make a deal.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Some say they were pressured not by a written order but by a message from the White House threatening an order. Marc Elias : He is trying to intimidate them. The way in which a mob boss intimidates people in the neighborhood. That he is seeking to either exact protection money from or engage in other nefarious conduct. I mean, the fact is that these law firms are being told, if you don't play ball with us, maybe something really bad will happen to you. Scott Pelley : The nine firms did not admit wrongdoing but altogether they agreed to give nearly $1 billion in legal services to causes that the firms and Trump support. Donald Ayer : Our whole system of government is at stake.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Scott Pelley : Attorney Donald Ayer should know he argued before the Supreme Court for the Reagan administration. He was Deputy Attorney General for George HW Bush. Donald Ayer : And that's their argument. And what anybody... Scott Pelley : Today he teaches at Georgetown Law. Donald Ayer : The idea that the president would issue executive orders aimed at any either specific person or organization, and stating that they're being punished because they're doing things that are politically disapproved by the people in power. That- that is completely unprecedented. Scott Pelley : Nobody has that right, including the president.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Donald Ayer : No, absolutely not. I think the president... President's an elected person and he has the right to do a great many things. But he doesn't have the right to essentially cancel out your right to have a lawyer of your choosing represent you in court by scaring the lawyer through threats that their personal livelihood will be destroyed. Scott Pelley : Now, America's legal community is torn between those who want to fight and those who made a deal. One firm that reached an agreement with Trump was Skadden Arps. Scott Pelley : Where Attorney Brenna Frey resigned in protest.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Brenna Frey : I think the message it sends to the country is power is what matters. If you have power, you can exercise that power however you want. And if that's true, why have a legal system at all? Why have law firms or lawyers at all? Scott Pelley : You thought that Skadden would fight? Brenna Frey : Because that's a foundational principle of the firm. That we are zealous advocates for the law. Scott Pelley : Why did this mean so much to you that you felt you had to quit? Brenna Frey : The law firm is tacitly saying, we'll, listen to the administration. We won't fight in court. If we won't fight over this what else won't we fight over in court against the federal government?

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Scott Pelley : In a note to its staff, Skadden Arps called its deal with Trump extraordinarily difficult but the best path to protect our clients, our people, and our firm. Brenna Frey : I think that they're naive if they think this makes the issue go away. Brenna Frey : There was nothing in these agreements that prevents the president from issuing another executive order against the law firm in the future. Donald Ayer : Someone must stand up to this because it is a direct attack on the whole functioning of our judicial system.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Scott Pelley : Four firms are standing up and fighting in court. Judges protected them with temporary restraining orders. Law Professor Donald Ayer says in his view, Trump's orders violate the constitutional rights to free speech, due process, and the right to counsel. Donald Ayer : Everyone's got a right to a lawyer, everyone's got a right to go to court, and it's something we've always assumed to be true and now it's threatened. Scott Pelley : So if the president targets a few specific law firms, the message to law firms across the country, in a nutshell, is what?

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Donald Ayer : I think the message is, that this can happen to you. But it's a real effort to prevent zealous representation of your client's legal interest when that results in something unacceptable to the administration. John Keker : You're at the mercy of the government and it, it really, it's like a protection racket. Scott Pelley : John Ecker is a prominent attorney and Democrat in San Francisco. You're not suggesting that the president's running a protection racket?

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: John Keker : I am. I'm, I'm, I'm suggesting that he is, uh, violating the rule that says you can't offer a thing of value in return for an official act. That happens to be the definition of bribery. Anybody else who came to Washington and said, I will give you a hundred million dollars of free legal services if you do this for me, would be convicted of a bribe. Scott Pelley : Ecker is helping recruit law firms nationwide to fight back. More than 500 firms, large and small have signed up in support.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: John Keker : We don't have to agree on politics but we do have to agree that the legal profession has to protect the rule of law in the United States. Which means lawyers and judges need to be independent from the executive branch. [Yes; see Ex parte Garland, 71 U.S. 333 (1866) ] Scott Pelley : If the president brings the legal profession to heal, what situation is the country in then? John Keker : No rule of law. You're in a dictatorship. That's what happened in China, it happens in Russia, these are legal systems that look like legal systems, but in fact are controlled by a dictatorship. President Trump : I just think that, uh, the law firms have to behave themselves.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Scott Pelley : Trump's attack on the law firms has been described by a federal judge as a personal vendetta. None of his targets is charged with any crime. Trump, however, was indicted by federal grand juries in cases about the 2020 election and allegedly concealing classified documents. He pleaded not guilty. Those prosecutions were dropped only because he was reelected. Last year, a state jury convicted him of falsifying business records, making him the first felon in the Oval Office.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: President Trump : I've been targeted for four years longer than that. So you don't tell me about targeting. I was the target of, uh, corrupt politicians for four years and then four years after that, uh... So don't talk to me about targeting. Scott Pelley : In Trump's defense government lawyers argue in court that his orders against the firms ensure that tax money is not supporting unlawful or unsavory practices. Another filing says the executive branch is merely managing who it does business with, not punishing anyone. And the government argues that the orders are "well within the scope of presidential prerogative."

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: President Trump : Well, the law firms all wanna make deals. You mean the law firms that we're going after that went after me for four years, ruthlessly, violently, illegally. You mean the... Are those are law firms you're talking about? They're not babies. They're very sophisticated people. Uh, those law firms did bad things. Bad things. They went after me for years. Uh, Russia, Russia, Russia hoax, all a hoax.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Scott Pelley : What Trump means by a hoax were allegations in 2016 of shady dealings with Russia by Trump and his campaign. He's right that the FBI could not corroborate what was described as rumor. At least one allegation was promoted to the media by Clinton campaign representatives when Mark Elias was general counsel. In this memo, six weeks ago, Trump says Elias is an example of grossly unethical misconduct. The President directs the Attorney General to seek sanctions against any lawyer anywhere for unreasonable and vexatious litigation against the government. Unreasonable apparently, in the eye of the president.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Scott Pelley : Are we reaching a point where a person will go to a law firm with a case that is opposed to the president of the United States, and the law firm will think, do we really want to take this case? Or not bring- taking on certain kinds of causes that might put them in the crosshairs of the administration. Scott Pelley : If lawyers give up their independence, what is lost?

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Marc Elias : The rule of law. And this is why the business community ought to care. So the legal system is fundamental to how our society operates, how capitalism operates, and everyone should have a stake in that. chunks.title: Neil 2028

chunks.text: Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook Share to Pinterest U.S. District Judge Pamela Chen : This concept of separation of powers is what makes America great. It is absolutely the genius of our democracy. U.S. District Judge James Boasberg : Here we are over two centuries later, and still the Constitution with its three pillars of government exists in the same form as it did at the founding. U.S. District Senior Judge Ann Montgomery : All of these parts working together creates a team effort, which really aids our form of government and creates its stability.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: U.S. District Judge James Boasberg : Many people don't realize that the Constitution sets out three branches of government. The first is the legislative branch. The second branch is the executive branch that we typically think of the President, but it also includes all of his executive officers. And the third is the judicial branch, and that means the Supreme Court, but it also means the United States Courts of Appeals and the United States District Courts. U.S. District Chief Judge Beryl Howell : Why would the framers want to set up such a complicated system that consisted of three branches of government with separate powers, but with some codependent powers?

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss : They were students of human psychology. U.S. District Senior Judge Reggie Walton : Because they appreciated that a free society does require diffusion of authority. Judge Moss: They said the right way to do this is to have checks and balances. Judge Howell : Each branch has designated powers, but some of those powers are codependent on cooperation with the other branches of government. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper : The process of passing a bill in the Congress requires a lot of debate and discussion and compromise.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Judge Montgomery : Congress, they can't act alone to create a law. It requires the President to approve the law. Of course, there's the veto power. Judge Cooper : If he vetoes it, it goes back to the Congress. And if they truly believe that the law should be passed, they can override that veto by a two-thirds vote. Judge Montgomery : Those laws are further held in check by the judicial review process to make sure that the law complies with our constitution.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Judge Cooper : If someone doesn't like that law, they can challenge it, um, and argue that it violates the Constitution and they can file a lawsuit in federal court. And if that happens, it's up to the judicial branch to decide whether the law complies with the Constitution or not. U.S. District Judge Reed O'Conno r: The judiciary is likewise checked by the other branches. Number one, it, it has no policy role in the government. It simply interprets the law. And so if a particular judge or circuit judges or the Supreme Court justices disagree with public policy, they have no say in that. They simply interpret the laws that come before them.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Judge Cooper : And if Congress passes a law that's challenged under the Constitution, the judiciary has the power to say, um, that law violates the Constitution and to strike it down. But that's not the end of the story. Judge Moss : Congress can come back and look for another way to try and achieve the same result in a fashion that is constitutional. And they've done that on many occasions in our history. We've got Congress and the President, and they're elected. Judge Chen : The President nominates us, and then the Senate confirms us. But the reason for that is so that we can retain our independence.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Judge Walton : The founders felt that the independence of the judiciary was critical, and one of the crucial ways we have that independence is through life tenure. Judge Chen : And we don't have to answer to Congress or to the White House or to the Executive Branch if we make a decision they disagree with. Judge Moss : When there is a decision from the Supreme Court that's not popular, sometimes that lack of popularity is exactly the way the system is supposed to be working. The example I'll give you there is flag desecration.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Judge Walton : There was legislation that precluded the burning of a flag. Obviously, the Executive Branch sought to enforce that legislation, and then it ultimately became the responsibility of the courts to make an assessment as to whether that legislation was constitutional. Judge Boasberg : No one's in favor of burning a flag, but the idea is that the Supreme Court believes that the Constitution protects everyone's liberties even for speech you don't like. Judge Moss : And that's what the First Amendment is about. And it's through the separation of powers that we're able to protect that.

chunks.title: Neil 2028
chunks.text: Judge Cooper : The courts are the ultimate guardians of the law. We don't have the power of the purse. We don't have an army. Our only power is our ability to defend the Constitution. Judge Chen : The reason we endure is because we have a system that ensures through these three separate branches of government that check and balance each other all the time, that all of us are protected by a single system that seeks to ensure fairness, liberty, and justice for everyone. chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Senator Ileana Garcia’s Legislative Record Senator Garcia has been a tireless champion, getting real results to make our community a better place. Whether she is securing millions in funding for local infrastructure and flood mitigation or fighting for the protections of our most vulnerable residents, Ileana Garcia’s legislative record clearly shows that she is always working hard and fighting for you. SB 186 Companion Bill Passed CS/CS/HB 1201 Protecting vulnerable students by updating requirements for response training for all school staff who interact with students with epilepsy. Ensuring our schools and teachers are properly equipped. (read more)

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: requirements for individualized seizure action plans (ISAPs) and expanding who must receive training. Schools must now ensure that all employees who regularly interact with a student, including classroom teachers, transportation staff, and activity supervisors, must complete seizure recognition and response training, which is valid for five years. The law also requires schools to display a seizure response poster and directs the Department of Education to identify approved free training courses and posters from national epilepsy organizations. These updates ensure that every student with epilepsy has a safer, more supportive learning environment.

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Fortifying Florida's coastlines using nature-based solutions like mangrove restoration and living seawalls. This allows smart, targeted environmental improvements in vital areas like Biscayne Bay to naturally protect our communities. (read more)

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: We advanced Florida's commitment to coastal resiliency by expanding the use of nature-based solutions to protect vulnerable coastlines like living shorelines, mangrove restoration, and hybrid green-gray infrastructure. The law authorizes carefully limited dredging and shoreline improvements within the Terra Ceia and Biscayne Bay Aquatic Preserves when they enhance environmental quality, public health, or coastal resiliency. It also allows structures such as living seawalls, wave-attenuation devices, and seagrass or vegetation plantings to strengthen natural defenses. Geoengineering and Weather Modification Activities

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Florida leads the way with this groundbreaking law banning unauthorized geoengineering and weather modification. Violators face serious consequences, ensuring the environment is protected for future generations. (read more)

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: We passed a first-in-the-nation law to prohibit unauthorized geoengineering and weather modification activities in Florida. Violators face felony penalties, and aircraft operators involved in such activities can be fined and imprisoned. The Department of Environmental Protection must now investigate public reports and coordinate with health and emergency agencies when needed. Public airports must report aircraft equipped for weather modification, and state funds will be withheld from those that don’t comply—ensuring transparency and environmental accountability.

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: A monumental stride in supporting students facing homelessness and those aging out of foster care, this law mandates that colleges provide essential housing resources, ensuring no young adult is left behind. (read more)

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: We took action to prioritize housing for students who are homeless or have aged out of foster care by requiring colleges and universities to give them first access to dorms, year-round housing, and work-study opportunities. The law removes barriers like cosigner requirements and strengthens support through the Foster Youth to Independence (FYI) initiative. It also requires agencies to help young adults secure leases and provide written assurances to landlords. A statewide study will identify remaining housing barriers, with findings due in 2026 to guide future improvements. Tampering with an Electronic Monitoring Device SB 1054 Companion Bill Passed CS/CS/HB 437

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: By reclassifying the crime of tampering with electronic monitoring devices, we enhance accountability, ensuring justice prevails, and communities are kept safe from those who aim to evade the law. (read more)

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: We strengthened public safety by expanding and reclassifying the crime of tampering with electronic monitoring devices. The law now includes anyone who helps or solicits others to interfere with monitoring, and penalties increase based on the severity of the underlying offense. Juveniles who tamper with devices also face felony charges, and courts must revoke pretrial release for offenders unless strict conditions are met. These changes ensure accountability and protect communities from those who attempt to evade justice. CS/CS/SB 192 Companion Bill Passed CS/CS/HB 437

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Expanding anchoring limitation areas in Biscayne Bay helps preserve our delicate marine ecosystems while ensuring safe boating practices. (read more) We expanded anchoring limitation areas in Biscayne Bay to protect sensitive marine environments and improve waterway safety. The new zones include areas between Palm Island and State Road A1A, and between San Marino and Di Lido Islands in Miami-Dade County. The law also allows boaters to use GPS tracking devices as proof of compliance and clarifies how to document vessel movement. These updates help balance environmental protection with responsible boating. Motor Vehicle Parking on Private Property

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: CS/CS/SB 388 Companion Bill Passed CS/CS/HB 271 Drivers deserve fairness! This law establishes vital protections for those using private parking lots, including clear signage and a fair appeals process. (read more) We passed strong consumer protections for drivers using privately-owned parking lots. The law requires clear signage, a 15-minute grace period, and a fair dispute and appeal process before late fees can be charged. It also prohibits the sale of personal information collected from parking services and ensures invoices are issued promptly and transparently. These reforms protect consumers from predatory parking practices while preserving property rights.

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: CS/CS/CS/SB 536 Companion Bill Passed HB 7089 Aiming for better accountability in child welfare, this law mandates transparency among agencies, ensuring our children receive the best possible support and preserving their welfare. (read more) We passed a new law to bring greater transparency and accountability to Florida’s child welfare system. It strengthens oversight of community-based care lead agencies (CBCs), which are responsible for delivering services to vulnerable children and families.

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Now, CBC board members must complete annual training and disclose any conflicts of interest. If they don’t, there are strict penalties—including fines and removal from the board. The law also requires CBCs to competitively bid contracts over $35,000, even with related parties, to prevent favoritism and misuse of funds.

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: To protect taxpayer dollars, the law caps executive salaries and ensures that any property bought with state funds can’t be sold or transferred without approval. It also directs the Department of Children and Families to work with providers to create a fairer, more efficient funding model that supports prevention, family preservation, and long-term stability for children. This legislation ensures Florida’s child welfare system is more accountable, more transparent, and focused on doing what’s right for kids.

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: A law to expand aftercare services to ages 18–22, helping former foster youth transition to independence. We also empowered the state to distribute emergency funds during crises, ensuring young adults have a safety net when they need it most. (read more)

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: We expanded eligibility for aftercare services to more young adults who spent time in foster care after age 14 but didn’t reunify with their families. Now, youth ages 18–22 can access critical support as they transition to independence. The law also allows the Department of Children and Families to distribute federal funds during emergencies to eligible young adults, even if they don’t meet standard criteria. This ensures no one is left behind in times of crisis. CS/CS/SB 1188 Companion Bill Passed CS/HB 1561

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Raising the bar for high-risk cosmetic procedures by enforcing stricter financial responsibility and insurance requirements. These reforms hold physicians accountable and limit where dangerous surgeries can take place to protect patient lives. (read more)

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: We strengthened safety standards for high-risk cosmetic procedures like liposuction and gluteal fat grafting. Physicians must now register their offices with the Department of Health and meet strict financial responsibility requirements, including liability insurance or a letter of credit. The law also limits where certain procedures can be performed and increases penalties for violations. These reforms protect patients and raise the bar for accountability in office-based surgery settings.

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: With a deep commitment to our elders, this law introduces tough penalties for those who exploit our seniors. It creates a robust framework that allows victims to seek justice and protect their hard-earned resources. (read more)

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: We passed a strong new law to protect Floridians aged 65 and older from financial exploitation through deception, intimidation, or abuse of trust. The law creates serious penalties for those who defraud seniors—up to a first-degree felony depending on the amount stolen—and allows victims to seek protective injunctions. It also extends the time prosecutors have to bring charges in cases involving fraud or breach of fiduciary duty, ensuring justice can still be served even if the crime is discovered years later.

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Making sure every taxpayer dollar counts! Nonprofits receiving state funds must disclose executive salaries, promoting transparency and accountability in the use of public resources. (read more) To ensure fiscal accountability, we now require nonprofits that receive state funds to publicly disclose how much of that money is used to pay their board members and executives. This information must be posted on the Florida Accountability Contract Tracking System (FACTS) and on the nonprofit’s website. Taxpayers deserve to know how their dollars are being spent—and this law delivers that transparency. Children and Young Adults in Out-of-home Care

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Named the Nancy C. Detert Champion for Children Act, this law empowers young individuals in foster care, ensuring they receive the necessary support and knowledge about their rights to thrive. (read more) Named the Nancy C. Detert Champion for Children Act, this law strengthens protections and support for children and young adults in out-of-home care. It creates the Office of the Children’s Ombudsman, ensures youth receive age-appropriate education about their rights and safety, and expands access to the Keys to Independence program, helping more foster youth get driver’s licenses. These changes empower young people with the tools and information they need to succeed.

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: This comprehensive legislation ensures fairness and transparency in securing collateral protection insurance for homeowners, preventing overcharging and abusive practices. (read more)

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: We passed a comprehensive law to regulate Collateral Protection Insurance (CPI) on real property, ensuring fair pricing and transparency for homeowners when lenders place insurance on their behalf. The law prohibits abusive practices like profit-sharing between insurers and lenders, requires clear evidence of coverage to be provided to homeowners, and mandates that CPI premiums be based on accurate property values. These reforms help prevent overcharging, protect consumer rights, and bring greater accountability to the mortgage insurance process.

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Modernized the Child Support Program to be more efficient and supportive. New rules allow parents in job training to defer payments, fix out-of-state credit issues, and removing outdated rules – helping families get support without the red tape. (read more)

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: We passed a comprehensive update to Florida’s Child Support Program to make it more efficient, accurate, and supportive of both children and caregivers. The law allows parents in job training to defer payments, ensures proper crediting of out-of-state payments, and removes outdated rules that penalized incarcerated parents. It also streamlines how clerks manage payments and fees, helping families receive the support they deserve without unnecessary delays.

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Ensuring confidentiality for peer support and allowing PTSD diagnoses via telehealth for workers’ compensation. We also extended the mental health commission’s work to study and improve critical services like the 988 crisis line. (read more)

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: We strengthened protections for first responders by expanding confidentiality for peer support communications and allowing PTSD diagnoses via telehealth for workers’ compensation claims. The law ensures that all peer supporters—whether active, volunteer, or retired—receive equal legal protections. It also extends and expands the state’s mental health commission, directing it to study suicide prevention services like the 988 crisis line and recommend improvements. These reforms help ensure Florida’s first responders and communities have access to the mental health support they need. Step into Success Workforce Education and Internship Pilot Program

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: This new three-year pilot gives foster youth ages 16–25 paid internships, mentorship, and workforce education. It provides financial stability, giving them the skills to thrive independently. (read more)

chunks.title: Legislation | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: We created the Step into Success Act, a three-year pilot program that helps foster and former foster youth ages 16–25 build professional skills and gain real-world work experience. The program includes workforce education, mentorship, and paid internships, with monthly financial assistance that doesn’t affect eligibility for other benefits. Participants are matched with mentors in partnering organizations and can earn postsecondary credit for their experience. chunks.title: Ileana Garcia working to secure additional funds to improve Biscayne Bay spoil islands | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Ileana Garcia working to secure additional funds to improve Biscayne Bay spoil islands | Ileana Garcia Ileana Garcia working to secure additional funds to improve Biscayne Bay spoil islands October 25, 2021 | by Jesse Scheckner on Florida Politics The man-made islands are rife with man-made trash. They’re also eroding due to illegal activity. It’s no secret Biscayne Bay is in trouble, and Sen. Ileana Garcia is now working with Miami-Dade County Chief Bay officer Irela Bagué to address one issue that has grown worse since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic: the deterioration of state-owned spoil islands in the bay.

chunks.title: Ileana Garcia working to secure additional funds to improve Biscayne Bay spoil islands | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: The remnants of past bay dredging, spoil islands are small, manmade land masses in the bay. Many today function as miniature beaches and parks complete with sand, mangroves and sea grape, among other native flora, attracting boaters, jet skiers and other aquatic pleasure seekers, as well as an overflow of garbage and debris . The short-term solution to the island trash problem devised months ago by Bagué and the city of Miami, one of the municipalities in Miami-Dade to which the spoil islands have been deeded, was to double the number of weekly trash pickups.

chunks.title: Ileana Garcia working to secure additional funds to improve Biscayne Bay spoil islands | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: But that’s still not enough, and it does nothing to prevent island erosion and physical damage illegally grounded and tethered vessels are causing. Far more work needs to be done — and funded — said Eduardo Tamborrel , Garcia’s legislative aide, who confirmed the Republican Senator has been trying to secure additional funding to maintain and improve the islands. “The municipalities that are managing the islands, there needs to be more financing,” he told Florida Politics. “One of the things the Senator is doing is seeing how she can facilitate helping with the financing of the organizational aspects.”

chunks.title: Ileana Garcia working to secure additional funds to improve Biscayne Bay spoil islands | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: In mid-August, Garcia participated in a workshop Bagué hosted to review the spoil island contracts deeded to Miami and other cities. Much of the workshop focused on curbing illegal charter vessels and livery operations. “Vessels that are illegally grounded or tied to trees are contributing to erosion and physical damage on the spoil islands in Biscayne Bay,” Garcia said in a written statement. “We must do all we can to protect and preserve these tranquil islands that provide our residents and visitors the opportunity to enjoy Florida’s unique natural resources away from the hustle and bustle of Miami’s dynamic urban environment.”

chunks.title: Ileana Garcia working to secure additional funds to improve Biscayne Bay spoil islands | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: To that end, Bagué said, locals and visitors must do their part to maintain the islands and cease “illegal activity, excessive use, irresponsible behavior, and a blatant disregard for nature and our unique wildlife.” “We must all take responsibility and treat Biscayne Bay and these spoil islands the same as we would our backyard, “she said in a statement, adding that the county is working with Garcia, law enforcement and local governments to increase enforcement and prohibit certain uses on the islands. “For decades, Miami-Dade County has spent millions of taxpayer dollars to restore these natural areas and pays weekly for removing trash and debris left behind.”

chunks.title: Ileana Garcia working to secure additional funds to improve Biscayne Bay spoil islands | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Biscayne Bay faces myriad other problems, including seagrass die-off , a record number of manatee deaths this year and repeated, devastating fish kills in the bay caused by wildly fluctuating temperatures and algal blooms . There’s also the increased toxification of the bay due to numerous sewage spills , leaking septic tanks — a multibillion-dollar problem for Miami-Dade County — and stormwater runoff flooding the bay with fertilizer, plastics and other pollutants. A lack of fresh water is also causing the waterway to suffer from “hyper salinity,” Bagué wrote in a nearly three-year-old Miami Herald op-ed .

chunks.title: Ileana Garcia working to secure additional funds to improve Biscayne Bay spoil islands | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Over the last several years, Garcia’s office said, the Florida Senate has made “unprecedented investments” in Florida’s natural resources, including Biscayne Bay. That included l egislation in April , which Garcia championed, to establish a nine-member Biscayne Bay Commission to oversee public projects and bay rehabilitation. In the 2021 Legislative Session, Garica secured $36 million for coastal resilience and Biscayne Bay — $20 million for bay restoration and preservation projects and $16 million in resiliency grant funding for South Florida.

chunks.title: Ileana Garcia working to secure additional funds to improve Biscayne Bay spoil islands | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: She’s now supporting Miami in establishing a slow speed minimum wake zone near the Miami Marine Stadium , increasing police presence on the Miami River to enforce existing speed zones and working to help law enforcement get additional resources to improve efforts. Boat propeller scarring is a “major threat” to seagrass beds, causing permanent scarring in some cases and destruction in worse ones, according to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection . “We’ve lost a lot of seagrass in the bay,” Tamborrel said.

chunks.title: Ileana Garcia working to secure additional funds to improve Biscayne Bay spoil islands | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Collision with watercraft also accounts for up to 25% of reported manatee mortalities, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission found. And when the peaceful sea creatures don’t die from a collision, they can still suffer sharp and blunt force trauma with lifelong effects. In a 10-year study, only 4% of manatees the Fish and Wildlife Research Institute came across were without watercraft-related scars.

chunks.title: Ileana Garcia working to secure additional funds to improve Biscayne Bay spoil islands | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: “It appears exceedingly rare for an adult manatee to not be struck multiple times in its life,” the organization said. “(Manatees) are subjected to more sublethal watercraft strikes than any other studied marine mammal and it underscores the need for continued long-term vigilance in conservation actions in Florida.”

chunks.title: Rationing the American Dream | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Rationing the American Dream | Ileana Garcia The Socialist Revolution once dismissed as the radical rantings of Bernie Sanders and the Squad have now become the marching orders for Democrats across the country. Led by Joe Biden and his handlers and underscored by violence in our streets, the march toward socialism may not come with a Ridgeway cap or an armed military, but it will most certainly result in the same devastating economic oppression experienced by millions around the world forced to exchange freedom for tyranny.

chunks.title: Rationing the American Dream | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: This revolution isn’t just promising a government takeover of health care and a free education. Their master plan is to nationalize our entire economy. Democrats argue that Medicare for All, education for all, housing for all and jobs for all will lead to economic and environmental justice for all. They want us to believe that the meat and medicine shortages in Venezuela can’t happen here. They praise Cuba’s literacy program while ignoring the fact that their technology is frozen in a pre-socialism state; and hope that we’re convinced that Americans standing, desperate and struggling to get by, in breadlines across the country are an impossibility in the 21st Century.

chunks.title: Rationing the American Dream | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: But a top-down driven economy by which government creates and rations everything from healthcare to education, and the distribution of jobs and housing is the definition of Market Socialism and the core of what extremists and the Democrats have planned for the American people. The government-dictated rationing of healthcare, housing and jobs will not lead to quality healthcare, nor will it lead to safe housing or better jobs. Let’s examine for a moment how well government-rationed programs that dictate options for people in this country have fared historically.

chunks.title: Rationing the American Dream | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Look no further than the failure of our federal government to provide adequate healthcare to the more than nine million Veterans forced into the VA’s labyrinth of hospitals and clinics. Veterans continue to struggle with low access, poor service, antiquated operational systems and bureaucratic processes. Despite the best efforts of some well-intentioned U.S. Representatives, the system remains a cautionary example of what government rationing of healthcare would look like for all Americans if Democrats are successful in November.

chunks.title: Rationing the American Dream | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: As Howard Husock pointed out in The Atlantic last year, “Advocates have not been discouraged by the fact that violence and neglect led to the demolition of previous generations of public housing. Nor by the rats, leaks, mold, and lead paint that have now brought the New York City Housing Authority, by far the nation’s largest operator of public housing, under the oversight of a federal monitor.’ Who will monitor the federal government if Democrats are successful in their bid to spend 2.5 trillion dollars to build nearly ten million new government-rationed public housing units?

chunks.title: Rationing the American Dream | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: Sanders’ Jobs for All program is built on the misguided promises of government-rationed healthcare, free childcare for all and the Green New Deal, a program that allows the government to ration everything from how much we drive to the kinds of foods we eat. Think about that for minute. What kind of jobs are available at $15 an hour in the construction, healthcare and childcare industries? This flawed, market socialism-driven fantasy is guaranteeing you a job digging ditches, scrubbing hospital floors and changing diapers.

chunks.title: Rationing the American Dream | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: That’s not a criticism of the honest day’s work afforded by these jobs, but rather a reality check for the 19-year-old on the quad who’s romanticizing the benefits of socialism while disregarding its decimation of choice and free agency. I appreciate our young people’s wide-eyed optimism for a world where no one wants for anything, but shutter at the notion so many are willing to trade the endless opportunities in front of them for the fairytale being sold to them by snake oil salesmen masquerading as saviors.

chunks.title: Rationing the American Dream | Ileana Garcia
chunks.text: The Democrat party is trying to ration the American Dream and constrain how much our children should dare to achieve. They are asking us to put our faith and our livelihoods in the hands of government instead of each other, to trade hard work for government-rationed handouts and achievement for obedience. They are trying to convince us that America, the greatest experiment in the history of the world, has failed. Someone needs to remind today’s Democrats that prescribed uniformity is not equality, capping potential is not freedom, and demonizing achievement is not justice.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate Accessibility for everyone. Powered by MDW Communications For nearly three decades, one party has controlled Florida’s Legislature—and today holds a supermajority in both chambers. With that much power comes responsibility for the choices Tallahassee makes. This isn’t about party. It’s about accountability. When power goes unchecked, government can stop listening to the people it serves. I’m running because District 36 deserves a representative focused on the pressures families face every day: rising housing and insurance costs, the cost of living, and the growing threat of sea-level rise.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: I will measure every vote by one simple question: Who does this actually serve? My priorities are organized around three questions every Floridian should be able to ask of their government. When something in Florida breaks — the insurance market, the housing market, the budget — the question that matters is who is handed the bill — and too often, the answer is you. Property Insurance That Works for Policyholders +

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Florida’s property-insurance market was genuinely broken, and recent reforms did stabilize it — rates slowed, new carriers entered, and far fewer families are stuck with the state insurer of last resort. I will not pretend otherwise. But stability is not the same as affordability. Families here pay among the highest premiums in the country to insure their homes, with more than half of a typical premium going to hurricane coverage alone. And policyholders have spent years paying a surcharge on every bill for the unpaid claims left behind by the companies that collapsed — even as Tallahassee takes credit for rate cuts.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Reform the state insurance framework so that families hit by predictable losses can actually recover, rather than being left with denied claims and added fees. Demand transparency and fairness in how the cost of a company’s collapse ends up on your bill. Treat insurance as the cost-of-living emergency it is for this district, where the insurance bill is as urgent as the rent or the mortgage. Tax Fairness for Renters and Working Families +

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Florida already has one of the most regressive tax systems in the nation: it takes a far larger share of a working family’s income than of a wealthy household’s. As proposals move to cut homestead property taxes, we must raise the objection no one is raising on behalf of the majority of this district who rent: if the exemption only reaches homeowners but the lost revenue is replaced by a higher sales tax, you do not get relief — you get the bill twice: in your rent and in everything you buy. Insist that any tax change be measured by its effect on renters and working families, not only on homestead owners.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Oppose shifting the cost of tax cuts onto regressive sales taxes that fall hardest on those who can least afford them. Protect funding for the local services — first responders, parks, road maintenance — that a sudden revenue hole would put at risk. The Power Bill the State Has Its Hand On +

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: I will not insult you by pretending a state senator can lower the price of groceries or gas — those are set by national and global forces no one in Tallahassee controls, and any candidate who claims otherwise is not being straight with you. Your electric bill is different. Part of it is fuel and storm recovery, which the state does not set and the company cannot mark up. But part of it is a base rate and a guaranteed company profit that a state commission approves — and that guaranteed profit is among the highest granted to any utility in the country. The state’s own consumer advocate has put the cost of it in the hundreds of millions of dollars, drawn from customers’ bills.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: The commission that approved it is not even required by law to consider whether families can afford the result. Fight for legislation that requires the utility commission to weigh affordability for families — something current law does not require it to do. Be honest about the limits: a senator cannot set a rate or order a bill lowered, but a senator votes on who sits on that commission and on the laws that bind it. Hold the state accountable only for what it controls — the base rate, the guaranteed profit, and the rules — while telling the truth about the fuel and storm costs it does not.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Make sure a coming driver of your bill — the enormous power and water demands of new data centers — is paid by the companies that profit from them: no public subsidies, no tax exemptions, and no stranded costs left on the ratepayer when a site shuts down. Standing With Families as Sea Levels Rise +

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: A state senator cannot raise a single street above the water — that is the work of our cities, and they are doing it. But the State of Florida writes the insurance rules that decide whether a family whose home floods can recover, and the state funds the grant programs — what Tallahassee calls “resilience” — that pay for the pumps, drainage, and seawalls that help communities adapt. Those are decisions a state senator votes on. Fight every year to fund the state’s flood-protection grants and to bring those dollars home to District 36’s communities. Reform flood and property-insurance rules so families whose homes flood are not left to absorb the loss alone.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Make sure the state shows up as a partner to the communities already doing the hard work of adaptation. Repeal the law that deleted “climate change” from most of Florida’s statutes. A state cannot plan for a risk it will not name — and the market prices that denial into your premium.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: After the Surfside collapse took ninety-eight lives, the state did the right thing: it required older buildings to be inspected and to fund the repairs they had long deferred. No one should undo that. But the state ordered the repairs and built no way to help families pay for them — and now, as those costs come due, the only help for an owner facing a five- or six-figure assessment is a county loan they have to repay. Tallahassee mandated the cost and handed people a loan application. Build the state assessment-relief fund that does not exist, so families are not forced to sell homes they have lived in for decades to comply with a safety law.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Keep faith with the safety mandate while insisting the state share the cost of a decision it made. Be honest about what these assessments are: bills that were always coming, which the law brought into the open — and which families should not have to shoulder alone.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Here is something Tallahassee does not advertise. There are federal dollars — our own tax dollars — available to cover working people in this community who fall in the gap: earning too much to qualify for help and too little to afford a plan. The state turned that money down. So those dollars go to other states — and the cost of caring for the uninsured comes back to us anyway, in the county sales tax and property tax that keep our safety-net hospital open. We pay our federal taxes and watch the help go elsewhere; then we pay again, locally, to cover the gap here at home. This is arithmetic, not ideology: we pay twice — once to Washington, once to the county — and get nothing back for it.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Fight to bring our own federal dollars home to cover working families in the coverage gap, rather than sending those dollars to other states. Be straight about the limits: when Washington let health-insurance subsidies lapse, premiums jumped here higher than almost anywhere — and a state senator cannot put a federal subsidy back. I will say so plainly, and fight for the state-level steps that could cushion it. Treat the cost of the uninsured as what it is — a charge already sitting on your county taxes, whether or not anyone admits it.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Some issues call for statewide standards. But Tallahassee shouldn’t dictate every decision to every community. Our cities and neighborhoods know their needs best. I’ll fight to keep local decisions local—and make sure the people closest to the problem have a real voice in solving it, and that is you.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: By the counts kept by Florida’s cities and counties, the Legislature has filed dozens of bills each session restricting the authority of local governments — on wages, on scheduling, on rent, on housing, even on protecting outdoor workers from the heat — and more. Most fail; but the Legislature files them again and again, session after session, year after year, and the ones that pass do real damage, including penalties aimed at the local officials who dare to cross Tallahassee. This is not a complaint about any single law. It is a pattern: a steady transfer of self-government to the capital.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Defend the constitutional home-rule authority of cities and counties against the relentless tide of preemption. Trust the officials closest to you — the ones whose offices you can walk into — to address the problems they know best. Be honest that the trend is not absolute: when the state has wisely left decisions in local hands, that judgment deserves to be defended and extended, not reversed.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Florida’s housing crisis is real, and the state’s signature housing law has produced some new homes and modestly narrowed the shortage. But it overrode local communities’ own planning to do so, and it has delivered only a small fraction of the housing the state needs. We can do better than seizing local control in exchange for a fraction of the fix. Support affordable-housing approaches that give communities a real say in what gets built in them. Hold large state housing programs accountable for results measured in homes families can actually afford. Protecting Communities’ Power to Adapt +

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: On flood and stormwater resilience, the state has so far left local governments the authority to act — which is why our cities have been able to write their own stronger building standards and protect their neighborhoods. That local authority is one of the few we still hold, and it is worth guarding. Protect local governments’ power to set stronger flood and storm-resistance standards from any future preemption. Defend Florida’s storm-resistant building standards from being weakened or repealed, and back the communities planning seriously for sea-level rise. Keeping Government Out of Private Life +

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: The same instinct that says the capital should not overrule your city says it should not reach into your home. Decisions about your family, your faith, and your private life belong to you — not to Tallahassee. Many of the families who built this district know from their own histories exactly what it costs when a government decides it may dictate who people are and how they must live. A government that respects its limits stays out of the places that were never its business. Defend the principle that the state has no place legislating your private life, your family, or your conscience.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Protect the separation of church and state — your right to practice your faith, or not, free of government pressure either way. Keep the focus of state power where it belongs: on the costs and decisions that are actually the state’s job, not on policing private life. Accountability is at the heart of good government. When one party controls every lever of power for too long, accountability disappears. Leaders stop listening, mistakes go unchecked, and voters pay the price.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: I’m running to bring accountability back to Tallahassee—and to make sure your voice is heard. We must break the stronghold Tallahassee has over the municipalities and counties and are not listening to the people they govern. Your voice is in your vote, and I would appreciate your confidence and support. Restoring Accountability to Tallahassee +

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Look honestly at what a generation of unchecked power has built. When the insurance market broke, the rescue went to the companies, and a surcharge went onto your bill. As tax changes advance, working families are being asked to pay for tax cuts they may never receive. And each time a community closest to you tries to act on your behalf, it is overruled or punished for crossing Tallahassee. None of this is an accident. It is what power that answers to no one does — it protects itself, and it sends the invoice to everyone else.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Consider the commission that sets the rules behind your power bill. The last time it denied the largest utility a rate increase was in 2010; the commissioners who cast that vote were denied reconfirmation and off the commission within months; and no commission has denied that company an increase in the years since. The people who said no were replaced, and the decisions have run one direction ever since. You can draw your own conclusion about who such a body answers to. Provide the check and balance that one-party supermajority control has erased — a vote and a voice that answer to this district, not to the capital.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Insist on transparency and real oversight of what state decisions cost working families. Measure every bill by a single test: does this serve the people of District 36, or the powerful interests closest to power? Following the Public’s Money in Our Schools +

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Florida now spends billions of public dollars on what the state calls private-school scholarships — vouchers, in plain terms — and on charter schools, and there is good in that record — families have used scholarships and their children have gone on to college, and competition has pushed some public schools to improve. I will not take that away. But the state has arranged the system so that the most basic accountability questions cannot be answered. Students who take scholarship money to attend private schools are not required to take the same statewide test that public schools are graded on, so no one can say whether the public is getting its money’s worth.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Charter schools are public, and their students take the same test — but when one closes, as hundreds have already, the state does not track why, or what happened to the students. And when public dollars are paid out as rent and fees to private operators, that money does not come back to the public school system if the charter school fails. Public money should be traceable. Right now, by the state’s own design, it is not. Require that public dollars spent on scholarships and charter schools be measured by results the public can actually see. Demand that the state track school closures, and account for the students and the public funds when a school fails.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Insist on transparency wherever public money flows to private operators, including the leases and management fees that ordinary families never get to see. This district was built in large part by families who know, from their own histories, exactly what it means when power runs only to the center and stops answering to the people. That instinct — that government should be close, accountable, and answerable — is not partisan. It is the oldest American idea there is. It is the idea I will carry to Tallahassee.

chunks.title: Why I Am Running — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: District 36 deserves someone in Tallahassee who answers to you, and only to you. That is what I am offering: I will show up, I will tell you the truth about what this office can and cannot do, and I will measure every vote by who it actually serves.

chunks.title: Meet George Lavín — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: I was born in Miami, and though my childhood took me overseas, every year I’ve spent in Florida I’ve spent right here in this community. My early childhood ran through Brussels and then Barcelona — where we landed in late 1975, just after the end of the dictatorship and the start of Spain’s return to democracy. The family then settled in Coral Gables in the early 1980s. I spent my school years here: St. Hugh Catholic School, Christopher Columbus High School (¡Adelante!), and my degree from FIU, after which I left for graduate school.

chunks.title: Meet George Lavín — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: After more than a decade away in New York — where I lived through the horror of 9/11 and saw firsthand the innate goodness of ordinary people in a time of terror — I returned to Florida twenty years ago, to Coral Gables and then to West Miami. As a legal consultant who works with former prosecutors, law firms, and corporate legal departments, I bring a sharp analytical mind and a deep sense of civic responsibility to everything I do.

chunks.title: Meet George Lavín — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: I come from people who kept having to leave — some pushed out by politics, some by need. My family’s roots run from Spain to Cuba and Canada. My father was born in Havana — a first-generation Cuban, but as Cuban as one could be. My mother was born in Montreal — where her family had gone after my grandfather, at just nineteen years old, fled Cuba to stay out of a Machado jail — and she was raised in Havana after they returned to Cuba. When the Revolution came, she was at university studying architecture — sadly, a degree she would never get to finish.

chunks.title: Meet George Lavín — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Her counterrevolutionary activities risked her arrest by the communist regime and made it impossible for her to stay; the Canadian government got her out — the same Canada that had taken my grandfather in a generation before — and she settled in New York, having to start from zero, like so many other exiles. My father was already an economist, a university graduate. He believed the Batista dictatorship had to be ousted, but broke with the change he’d wanted for Cuba when it turned to communism — one dictatorship traded for another. He, too, left for New York and also had to start from zero. Neither of them ever went back to Cuba.

chunks.title: Meet George Lavín — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: Two exiles, two anti-communists who raised four boys, above all, to question everything, show compassion, and live a moral life. It is a family history that taught me early what it costs when a government stops answering to the people it governs.

chunks.title: Meet George Lavín — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: I registered as a Democrat at eighteen — by conviction, not by inheritance, and not in spite of how I was raised but because of it. My parents, like their parents before them, poured everything into our education, and the schools they chose taught us to think for ourselves, serve others, and live a moral life. Over the years I watched my parents come to feel that the party they had long called home no longer reflected the principles they had held their whole lives. They taught me that principle comes before party — and that lesson is at the heart of why I am running.

chunks.title: Meet George Lavín — George Lavín for State Senate
chunks.text: My husband and I — married nine years — have built our life here, guided by the example of both our parents’ marriages, each lasting more than fifty-five years: proof that communication, compassion, and compromise can bridge almost any divide. Now I’m ready to give back — with new ideas, fresh energy, and an unwavering commitment to making every citizen and resident feel seen, heard, and represented. One party has held all the power in Tallahassee for too long, without having to answer to the people it governs. I’m running to make them answer.

chunks.text: George Lavín for State Senate · Florida District 36 Accessibility for everyone. Powered by MDW Communications George Lavín is running for State Senate to bring accountable, common-sense leadership to Tallahassee — the kind that listens first and delivers results. I was born in Miami and grew up in Coral Gables, where I attended St. Hugh, Christopher Columbus High School, and FIU. After graduate school and years in New York, I came home to South Florida twenty years ago. My husband and I have built our life here.

chunks.title: George Lavín for State Senate · Florida District 36
chunks.text: My parents fled Cuba after opposing dictatorship. They taught my brothers and me to question authority, show compassion, and put principle before party. That’s why I registered as a Democrat at eighteen, and it’s why I’m running today. As a legal consultant, I bring an analytical mind and a commitment to public service. Tallahassee has gone too long without answering to the people it governs. I’m running to make every resident feel heard and represented—and to hold those in power accountable. Common-sense priorities for our community A focused plan built on listening to neighbors across District 36.

"In Loving Memory of Ms. Betsie Gallardo"

chunks.title: Press Releases
chunks.text: In 2008, Betsie Gallardo was sentenced to a five-year sentence at Broward Correctional Institution for biting and kicking a Collier County sheriff’s deputy. Betsie was born HIV-positive and was an immigrant from Haiti. Due to her condition, she was sentenced to live out what was to be the remainder of her life in prison. In 2010, Betsie was diagnosed with late-stage cancer and made a last wish to live her remaining days outside of prison. Her adoptive mother, Jessica Bussert, who adopted Betsie 17 years ago on a mission trip, pleaded with legislators to release Betsie.

chunks.title: Press Releases
chunks.text: Upon hearing the case, Representative Campbell moved to get Betsie released. Shortly after, the Florida Parole Commission voted to approve Gallardo’s medical release from prison to live her remaining days outside. On Monday, January 31, 2011, Betsie Gallardo passed away surrounded by family and friends. Representative Campbell is glad Betsie was able to live out her remaining days with her family and wishes them the best. "I'm just overjoyed to take her home to Indiana to die with dignity.” -Jessie Bussert, Betsie’s mother

HB 61 requires each district school board’s code of conduct to include an explanation of student responsibilities regarding appropriate student dress.

chunks.title: Press Releases
chunks.text: The bill was introduced last year due to the increasing number of complaints about students coming to school dressed inappropriately. Campbell, an avid proponent of education, was dismayed by the varying student codes of conduct at Miami-Dade Public Schools. The codes of conduct often listed lax or sometimes nonexistent rules regarding appropriate dress.

chunks.title: Press Releases
chunks.text: The bill mandates that each district school board adopt a dress code policy that prohibits students from wearing clothing that exposes underwear or body parts in a specified manner and provides disciplinary actions for violations. Additionally, the bill requires students to adhere to the student conduct code during extracurricular activities. Representative Campbell is a staunch opponent of the distribution of the FCAT, the Florida Comprehensive Assessment Test. Campbell argues that the FCAT is not an adequate or fair way to measure a student’s abilities.

chunks.title: Press Releases
chunks.text: Campbell filed House Bill 71 in an effort to replace the FCAT with the High School Competency Test. This would assess a student’s ability based on the material they have learned during the past year, rather than a universal test given to students who learn different curricula. She believes that students need to be seen as individuals, rather than as part of a whole. Campbell criticizes the FCAT for contributing to the relatively low, yet improving, 70 percent graduation rate at schools like Miami Edison Senior High and Miami Central. She believes the FCAT places too much pressure and importance on a single test to accurately measure a student’s abilities.

chunks.title: Press Releases

chunks.title: Press Releases
chunks.text: Miami, Florida - On Yesterday, October 17, 2014, the Department of Homeland Security announced that they will begin implementation of a Haitian Family Reunification Parole (HFRP) Program to expedite family reunification for Haitian family members of U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents of the U.S. and to promote safe, legal and orderly migration from Haiti to the United States.

chunks.title: Press Releases
chunks.text: Under this program U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) will offer eligible Haitian beneficiaries of already approved family-based immigrant visa petitions, who are currently in Haiti, an opportunity to come to the United States up to approximately two years before their immigrant visa priority dates become current. This is great news that serves as a groundbreaking day in the Haitian community. Representative Campbell, herself has been working arduously and diligently to see that the HFRP comes to fruition. From multiple letters to diverse Press Releases this has been an issue Representative Campbell has fought and pushed for since her first term in office.

chunks.title: Press Releases
chunks.text: Representative Campbell goes on to say "This is an amazing day for constituents of district 108 and all other Haitian American families. It is a day that I have been fighting hard for since 2010 and since that time I have sent multiple correspondences to the White House and I have even passed legislation with the Florida House of Representatives to get this program introduced. I am overjoyed to celebrate this day along with all of the families that are soon to be reunited." Today proves that persistence overcomes all. Representative Campbell would also like to extend a warm thank you to President Obama for his position in implementing the HFRP.

chunks.text: Wancito Francius for State Representative District 108 Wancito Francius for State Representative District 108 "A lifelong resident fighting for the people of District 108 — committed to community, accountability, and a stronger future for every family." I'm Wancito Francius — a lifelong resident of District 108, and I'm running because our community deserves a representative who has lived our challenges and is ready to fight for our future.

chunks.title: Wancito Francius for State Representative District 108
chunks.text: I've seen firsthand the struggles families in our district face every single day — from the rising cost of living, to underfunded schools, to broken systems that no longer serve our people. I'm not running to occupy a seat. I'm running to deliver real, accountable representation that puts our community first. I believe we can build a better future for District 108 — one where opportunity is real, where every child has access to a quality education, and where families feel safe, supported, and seen. I'm asking for your trust, your voice, and your vote to help make that future happen.

chunks.title: Wancito Francius for State Representative District 108
chunks.text: A clear, focused agenda — built around the issues that matter most to the families, workers, and small businesses of District 108. Champion the entrepreneurs, workers, and local businesses who power our economy and keep our district thriving. Ensure our public schools are properly funded and every student has access to a quality education and a real shot at success. Enact Just & Humane Immigration Policies Stand for policies that are fair, lawful, and treat every family with the dignity and humanity they deserve. Heal our communities from trauma and rebuild trust between residents and the officers who serve and protect us.

chunks.title: Wancito Francius for State Representative District 108
chunks.text: Reform a system that has failed too many for too long — and replace it with one rooted in fairness, justice, and second chances. Take real, measured action to end the gun violence threatening our streets, our schools, and our children's futures. "I'm not running to occupy a seat — I'm running to deliver for the people of District 108." Beyond the core mission, here are the additional fights I'm committed to taking on for the people of District 108.

chunks.text: Wancito Francius is championing the Nathan Emmanuel Francius Autism Support and Resources Act — a landmark bill that would direct $8,000,000 in state funding to schools and behavioral health professionals serving children with Autism Spectrum Disorder across Florida. This is personal. This is purposeful. And this is what real representation looks like.
